prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "STRYKER CORP" (ticker SYK), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "SYK", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Stryker Corporation
result.industry: Medical technology (orthopaedics, surgical and neurotechnology devices)
markets: Knee and hip joint replacement (Mako robotic-assisted surgery)
Endoscopy, sports medicine and operating-room video
Hospital beds, stretchers, emergency care and nurse communication (Medical)
Neurovascular and peripheral vascular devices (including Inari)

mission.statement: Together with our customers, we are driven to make healthcare better.
mission.source: Stryker company website (stryker.com, Our company page)
mission.plain: Work hand in hand with doctors and hospitals to make medical care better for patients.

about.plain: Stryker makes the tools and parts doctors use to fix people's bodies. It makes new knees and hips, plates and screws for broken bones, and a robot arm called Mako that helps surgeons cut bone precisely. It also makes power saws and drills for surgery, cameras for keyhole operations, hospital beds and stretchers, and devices that pull clots out of blood vessels in the brain and legs. Hospitals around the world buy these products again and again.
about.customers: Hospitals, surgery centres, surgeons and emergency services buy its products.
about.everyday: If someone you know got a new knee or hip, rode on an ambulance stretcher or lay in a hospital bed, there is a good chance Stryker made it.

money.plain: power saws and drills, surgical navigation, endoscopy cameras and sports-medicine gear
artificial knees and hips, many placed with the Mako robot
beds, stretchers, defibrillators and nurse-call systems
plates, screws and implants for broken bones, shoulders, feet and ankles
tools and implants for brain, skull and ear-nose-throat surgery

money.part: Clot removal and blood vessels (incl. Inari)
money.plain: catheters that pull clots out of brain and leg vessels and stroke devices

result.summary: Stryker has a wide, durable advantage built on surgeon training and loyalty to its implants, an installed base of more than 3,000 Mako robots that ties hospitals to its knee and hip implants, and a huge sales force that sells hundreds of products across the operating room. The advantage is strongest in joint replacement, trauma and surgical equipment; it is weaker in vascular, where 2026 supply problems after a cyberattack cost share.

pricingPower.evidence: Price added only 0.4% to 10.3% organic growth in 2025 (volume 9.9%), and management expects 2026 pricing to be similar, positive in MedSurg and slightly negative in Orthopaedics, so growth comes from volume and mix (Mako, new products) rather than price increases; gross margin has held near 64% (64.0% in 2025) despite about $400M of expected 2026 tariff costs.

moats.evidence: Stryker, Mako, Triathlon knees and its surgical power tools are trusted brands among surgeons and hospital buyers, backed by large patent portfolios and decades of clinical data.

Over two-thirds of US knees and over a third of US hips Stryker sells were done on Mako by end-2025, and Mako only works with Stryker implants; surgeons trained on its instruments and hospitals with installed beds, tools and communication systems rarely switch.
More Mako cases generate more surgical data and training that improve planning software, but there is no true user-to-user network effect.

With $25.1B of 2025 sales, about 56,000 employees and customers in 61 countries, Stryker can spread R&D ($1.62B in 2025) and a large sales force over a broad portfolio, but its margins are not lower-cost than peers.
Large joint replacement is a concentrated market of a handful of players (Stryker, Zimmer Biomet, J&J DePuy Synthes, Smith+Nephew) where regulatory approvals and clinical history deter new entrants.
Stryker is an incumbent, and rivals such as Zimmer Biomet and Smith+Nephew have copied its model with their own robots (ROSA, CORI).
A decentralized, sales-driven culture and a record of integrating more than 60 acquisitions under Kevin Lobo (Mako, Wright Medical, Vocera, Inari) are hard to copy.
Mako robotic technology and patents are exclusive, but no single input is cornered.

customers.evidence: About 30-40% of hospitals now have more than one Mako, utilization reached about 50% of Stryker knees globally, and capital order books were elevated entering 2026, showing repeat purchases; the company says it serves more than 150 million patients a year.

talent.evidence: Stryker ranked No. 55 on Fortune's 2026 100 Best Companies to Work For, and its next CEO, Spencer Stiles, is a 27-year insider, showing deep internal bench strength.

product.evidence: Mako is the leading orthopaedic robot with more than 3,000 systems installed, Stryker says it is now the largest neurovascular player, and launches such as Mako 4 (hip, spine, shoulder), Triathlon Gold and the Pangea trauma platform keep the portfolio fresh.

competitors.note: Competes for hospital robotics and capital budgets; not in orthopaedics.

threats: Peripheral vascular (Inari) supply shortfalls after the March 2026 cyberattack are costing share to Penumbra and others, with a 70-80 basis point drag on growth expected again in Q4 2026.
Rival orthopaedic robots (Zimmer Biomet ROSA, Smith+Nephew CORI, J&J VELYS) could erode Mako's lead and the implant pull-through it creates.
Hospital budget pressure, European health-system funding strains and possible US reimbursement cuts could slow capital purchases and procedure growth.
Tariffs of about $400M expected in 2026 and slightly negative Orthopaedics pricing weigh on margins.
Integration risk from a steady stream of acquisitions (about $4.96B spent in 2025, mostly Inari).
CEO transition: Kevin Lobo hands over to Spencer Stiles on January 1, 2027.
Securities class-action solicitations after the July and September 2026 share drops.

ceo.name: Kevin Lobo (Spencer Stiles becomes CEO on January 1, 2027)
ceo.background: Chartered accountant with a McGill BCom and University of Toronto MBA; former president of J&J's Ethicon Endo-Surgery

c1.evidence: Stryker leads robotic-assisted joint replacement with more than 3,000 Mako systems installed, but orthopaedics and hospital equipment are established markets growing mid-single digits rather than emerging industries.

c2.evidence: Surgeons choose Stryker for Mako's precision, a full operating-room portfolio and a large, well-trained sales force; with over two-thirds of US Stryker knees done on Mako and 30-40% of hospitals owning more than one, that installed base is hard to copy and likely to last.

c3.evidence: Surgeons and hospital staff know Stryker as a default leader in orthopaedics and surgical equipment, but most ordinary consumers do not recognize the name the way they know Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci.

c4.evidence: Its mission, "Together with our customers, we are driven to make healthcare better," is repeated in its materials and values, and impacting more than 150 million patients a year matters, but it is a customer-service mission rather than a bold, transformational one.

c6.evidence: “quality, orthopaedics, Mako robot, sales-driven”: among doctors, hospitals and investors the impression is mostly positive, as a reliable, well-run medtech leader, though 2026's cyberattack and supply problems dented it.

c7.evidence: An aging population and rising joint replacement demand give a large, steadily growing market (management expects orthopaedic markets to grow mid-single digits), but it is not a fast secular trend like AI or cloud.

c8.evidence: Stryker keeps entering new markets through acquisitions, such as peripheral vascular via Inari in 2025, health IT via Vocera, and new Mako applications in spine and shoulder.

m1.evidence: Kevin Lobo pushed Stryker into robotics (Mako) and digital and set a clear growth-through-acquisition strategy, but he is a disciplined operator more than a futurist.

m2.evidence: Lobo is not a founder, but in 14 years as CEO he built for the long term, roughly tripling sales from $8.7B in 2012 to more than $26B, and hands over to a 27-year insider.

m4.evidence: Stryker's values (Integrity, Accountability, People, Performance) and its ranking on Fortune's 2026 100 Best Companies to Work For point to people-focused leadership, but there is little specific evidence of servant leadership.

m5.evidence: Stryker's decentralized, high-performance culture keeps launching products such as Mako 4, Triathlon Gold, Pangea trauma plates and Vocera badges, and spends about $1.6B a year on R&D.

m6.evidence: Lobo is a chartered accountant and finance-trained executive, not an engineer, though he ran J&J's Ethicon Endo-Surgery before Stryker.

m7.evidence: No scandals have marked Lobo's tenure, and he chairs a hospital trustee board and serves AdvaMed, but there is no clear evidence of a mission beyond running a strong medtech company.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Kevin Lobo at a top university was found.

m8b.evidence: Lobo is a low-profile, disciplined corporate leader without a distinctive public persona.

m9.evidence: Under Lobo sales roughly tripled from $8.7B (2012) to $25.1B (2025), adjusted EPS reached $13.63 in 2025, and he closed more than 60 acquisitions including Mako and Wright Medical.

m10.evidence: Stryker is not specifically known for frugality; SG&A is high at $8.65B, 34% of 2025 sales, typical of sales-heavy medtech.

c10.evidence: Stryker says its products reach more than 150 million patients a year in 61 countries, from joint replacements that restore mobility to stroke clot-removal devices and defibrillators.

p2.evidence: Making FDA-cleared implants, surgical robots and neurovascular catheters requires deep engineering, clinical evidence and regulatory work, and these products are vital to surgery and emergency care.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose every year from FY2021 to FY2025 ($17.1B, $18.4B, $20.5B, $22.6B, $25.1B) after a COVID dip to $14.4B in 2020.

f2.evidence: Operating margin rose from 15.5% in 2020 to 19.5% in 2025 but swung in between (16.3% in 2024 after $977M of impairments), while gross margin stayed roughly flat near 63-64%.

f3.evidence: Total debt of $14.9B far exceeds $3.5B of cash, but it is about 3 years of operating cash flow ($5.0B in 2025), interest is covered about 8x, and equity is a positive $24.0B (June 2026).

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $2.22B in 2020 to $4.89B in 2025 and operating cash flow from $3.28B to $5.04B, though cash flow dipped to $2.62B in 2022.

v1.evidence: Mako gives a clear, easy-to-explain reason to choose Stryker in knees and hips (robot-guided precision), but in many other categories its products are strong but not clearly superior.

v2.evidence: Stryker ranked No. 55 on Fortune's 2026 100 Best Companies to Work For list.

c5.evidence: Hospitals, surgeons and millions of patients needing joint replacements, trauma repair, stroke treatment and emergency care would miss its products, many of which are standard equipment in operating rooms and ambulances.
